newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan absent from Asia central bank meeting.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan absent from Asia central bank meeting.

text.p: When Asian central bankers gather in Shanghai on Friday to discuss the region's currency woes, one of the region's most powerful banks -- the Taiwan central bank -- will be conspicuously absent.

Sheu Yuan-dong, governor of the bank that boasts the world's third-biggest foreign exchange reserves, will not attend the meeting because Taiwan, despite a muscular and developed economy, remains an international pariah.
Taiwan says the meeting's host, China, is the culprit.
"The only reason we are not in the meeting is because China keeps imposing political pressure to keep us out of international activities," a Taiwan central bank official said.
"We are always interested in participating in any kind of regional affairs."

China, Taiwan's rival since they were split by civil war in 1949, says the island is a renegade province unqualified for international recognition and has aggressively sought to drive Taipei into oblivion.
The tactic has succeeded in large measure, and has extended from politics to the economic realm.
Despite unyielding attempts to break out of isolation, Taipei only has 30 diplomatic allies -- almost all of them impoverished small states dependent on its financial succour.

Although it fields one of the world's largest and most liberalised economies, this capitalist island of 21 million people has formal membership in just one international financial organisation -- the Asian Development Bank (ADB).

Taiwan has been frustrated for seven years in its bid to join the top international trade club, the World Trade Organisation, largely because communist-ruled China insists it must accede before Taipei.

It was during the 1997 ADB meeting in Japan in May that Taiwan central bank governor Sheu and People's Bank of China governor Dai Xianglong made a rare joint appearance, briefly allowing the two economic juggernauts to cross a formal path.

Such a meeting cannot occur in Shanghai on Friday because Taiwan does not belong to the 11-member Executive Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks, an institution modelled on the Bank for International Settlements.
"The issue of Taiwan does not arise since it is not a member of the group meeting on Friday," a People's Bank official said from Beijing.
Politics aside, Taiwan's membership would have made perfect economic sense.
Its central bank boasts an imposing foreign exchange war chest of US$90.008 billion -- the world's biggest after Japan and China.

While other central banks have foundered trying to stabilise their currencies against speculation, Taiwan has managed to curb speculation while still allowing a moderate fall in its currency to craft healthy export numbers.
Taiwan's export-driven economy posted a trade surplus of US$14.704 billion in 1996. Its gross domestic product showed a 6.83 percent annual growth in the first quarter of 1997.

The need for fresh regional cooperation on currencies was thrown into sharp relief on Tuesday when Malaysia reported an 8.8 billion ringgit ($3.32 billion), or 12.5 percent, fall in its foreign exchange reserves to 61.9 billion ringgit ($23.36 billion) in the first two weeks of July.
The Philippines, another member beset by speculative attacks on its peso, has less than US$12 billion of foreign exchange reserves at its disposal.
Sheu said last week that the Taiwan dollar was not vulnerable to the speculative pressures that have undermined several other southeastern currencies in July.
